name: Lotus extract

lead: Lotus extract comes from the sacred lotus and is used in K-beauty and other skincare as an antioxidant botanical. People use it for a calmer, brighter, healthier-looking complexion.

It is thought to work through antioxidant flavonoids and related plant compounds that protect skin. Two small 2013 studies in healthy adults tested topical lotus combined with green tea on facial wrinkles and oiliness.

paras: Applied as part of creams, serums and masks in a daily routine, usually combined with other botanicals such as green tea.
No specific cosmetic safety problems were identified in the sources reviewed. Blue lotus (Nymphaea) is a different plant with its own safety assessment.

angle.text: Sacred lotus extract is used in K-beauty skincare as an antioxidant botanical that calms and protects skin for a brighter look. Two small 2013 human studies tested it combined with green tea.

lead: Lotus extract is derived from the sacred lotus (Nelumbo nucifera), an aquatic perennial whose seeds, rhizomes and leaves have long been used in food and in folk, Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine [1]. In skincare it is used as an antioxidant botanical in serums and creams, with the aim of smoother-looking skin, fewer visible fine lines and a more matte, less oily finish [2][3].

The name is also applied to unrelated plants such as blue lotus (Nymphaea caerulea), which has different chemistry and is sold as tea and tincture [4]. Human research on lotus extract for skin is limited to two 2013 studies of small groups of healthy adults using green-tea-and-lotus emulsions, one on facial wrinkles and one on sebum [2][3]. Other lotus research is in animals or the laboratory [5][6].

paras: Sacred lotus has been cultivated for roughly 3,000 years, initially for its edible seeds, and China produces about 70 percent of the lotus eaten by people. Varieties are grouped as rhizome, seed or flower lotus according to their main use [1][1]. It is sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Chinese culture and symbolises purity and spiritual awakening [1].

Reported constituents include the flavonol miquelianin and benzylisoquinoline alkaloids such as nuciferine and neferine in leaves, and proteins, polyphenols, polysaccharides, B vitamins, vitamin E and superoxide dismutase in seeds. Rhizomes are about 31 percent starch [1][1]. Wikipedia notes that several medical claims about the plant need more reliable references [1].

Lotus extract is used in serums, creams and other leave-on skincare for its antioxidant content and as a botanical in K-beauty and herbal-leaning formulations. In the human studies below it was combined with green tea extract in multiple-emulsion formulations [2][3]. Product labels may list it as Nelumbo nucifera flower, leaf or seed extract.
The leaves' water-repellent waxy surface gave rise to the biomimetic term lotus effect, which concerns materials science and is unrelated to skincare [1].

Rhizomes, leaves and seeds have been used in folk medicine, Ayurveda and Chinese medicine, and seeds are still prepared in Chinese medicine as lian zi xin. Rhizome extracts have been studied for diuretic, anti-diabetic, antioxidant and antipyretic effects, though Wikipedia flags several of these claims as lacking adequate sourcing [1]. Lotus rhizome, seeds and stems are also eaten across Asia, and raw consumption carries a risk of parasite transmission, so cooking is advised [1].

A 2013 study in Rejuvenation Research enrolled 33 healthy Asian men in a placebo-controlled split-face design. One group used a multiple emulsion with green tea, a second with lotus extract, and a third with both, applying the active to one side of the face and placebo to the other once daily for 60 days. Skin was measured with the Visioscan VC and surface evaluation software at baseline and on days 30 and 60. The authors reported significant improvements in roughness, scaliness, smoothness and wrinkling, for example a 49.99 percent improvement in smoothness from baseline [2].

A 2013 single-blinded, placebo-controlled, split-face study in Hippokratia with 22 healthy adults compared green tea and green tea plus lotus emulsions against placebo for control of sebum secretion [3]. Both studies tested lotus in combination with green tea, in small samples, with cosmetic imaging endpoints. No large independent trials were found.

A water extract of lotus seed was reported to promote non-REM sleep in rats through GABAergic receptors [5]. An ethanolic extract of lotus leaves showed free-radical scavenging, iron-binding and anti-hemolytic properties in laboratory work using HepG2 cells [6]. A 2023 survey and safety assessment of blue lotus (Nymphaea caerulea) extracts examined a different species sold as tea and tincture [4]. A registered trial of a lotus seed and rice germ blend on sleep in menopausal women is listed as not yet recruiting [7].

timeline.event: A lotus seed about 1,300 years old is germinated [1].
Two small studies test green tea plus lotus emulsions on facial wrinkles and sebum [2][3]; the lotus genome is also sequenced [1].
